New to powerlifting?

Here’s how to read the numbers.

This is competition data, not a survey of every woman who strength trains. The same athlete can appear more than once because she may compete at several meets over time.

01

One row = one competition entry

Each row describes one woman lifting at one competition on one date.

02

“Total” means the lifts added together

For a three-lift meet, the total is her best successful squat, bench press, and deadlift, measured in kilograms.

03

Event codes describe the lifts

SBD means squat, bench press, and deadlift. Other codes represent one lift or a smaller combination.

04

Support and organizers are categories

Equipment describes supportive gear such as wraps or a lifting suit. A federation is the organization running or recording the competition—not a country.

01 / 03
Finding one · scale over time

The women’s record is broad—and still growing.

The prepared analysis contains — women’s meet records across — years. The yearly series shows the number of records available in the balanced analysis slice, not a population estimate.

The source archive contains more than four million total rows. This site uses a deterministic women-only slice capped per year so the browser dashboard stays fast.

02 / 03
Finding two · event context

A three-lift total is not the same as one lift.

The archive includes full competitions and single-lift events. A full SBD result includes squat, bench press, and deadlift, while a bench-only result measures just one lift.

Use “Full meets · SBD” in the dashboard when you want the clearest apples-to-apples comparison.

03 / 03
Finding three · equipment matters

Supportive gear changes the comparison.

Some competitors lift with little supportive equipment, while others use wraps, lifting suits, or more supportive gear. Those categories appear together in the archive, but they should not be treated as one universal leaderboard.

The dashboard lets you compare one support category at a time.

Methods & limitations

Useful data needs honest boundaries.

What one row means

One row represents one female lifter in one competition. Dates, event codes, equipment, bodyweight, lift results, federation, and meet fields come from the public source.

What we changed

Names were replaced with stable anonymous athlete IDs. The analysis uses a deterministic, year-balanced reservoir sample capped at 2,500 women’s records per year.

What this cannot prove

Competition records do not represent every woman who strength trains. They cannot establish causation, training quality, or a universal ranking across different events and equipment.

Source: OpenPowerlifting Data Service. The dataset is updated by its maintainers; this analysis was generated from the archive used in the repository.
